title: Astronomers Uncover a Mysterious Magnetic Web Above the Sun
summary:
Above the parts of the Sun that look calm, astronomers have found a hidden web. Using a balloon-borne observatory called Sunrise-III, an international team led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan discovered a surprisingly complex network of thin, thread-like magnetic structures above a quiet region of the Sun.

Quiet regions cover most of the Sun, but quiet does not mean magnetically inactive. Their magnetic fields are generally weaker than those in active areas, and their fine structures are hard to measure from the ground, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere blurs the details.

Sunrise-III was built to rise above that problem. During its 2024 mission, a high-altitude balloon carried its 1-metre telescope to about 35 kilometres above Earth, into the stratosphere, where atmospheric interference is greatly reduced.

There, the observatory studied the magnetic canopy, a network of magnetic fields that extends through the chromosphere, the layer of the solar atmosphere above the Sun's visible surface, the photosphere. Surface magnetic fields spread outward and arch upward, but the new observations show the canopy is not smooth and uniform. Instead, it contains many narrow, thread-like features woven into the larger network.

Computer simulations that reproduced the patterns seen by Sunrise-III suggest surface movements twist magnetic field lines, creating the intricate structures higher up.

The observatory also looked at another quiet region near the Sun's visible edge, the limb. There it measured magnetic fields inside spicules, narrow jets of solar material that shoot upward from the surface, showing how the field changes with height.

SCIP, the Sunrise Chromospheric Infrared spectroPolarimeter, developed under Japanese leadership, measures magnetic fields continuously from the photosphere to the chromosphere. Understanding this tangled canopy could help scientists investigate how energy from motions near the surface is transferred into higher layers.
why_it_matters: Understanding the Sun's magnetic web matters because energy moving through its layers shapes solar activity, and clearer models of that process help scientists study our nearest star.

background_read: The Sun is a star, and like Earth it has a magnetic field, an invisible force that can push and pull magnetic material.
The visible surface of the Sun is called the photosphere, and the layer above it is the chromosphere.
Earth's atmosphere can blur views from the ground, so telescopes are sometimes carried high above most of the air to see more clearly.
By studying magnetic fields, scientists try to learn how energy moves from the Sun's surface into its outer layers.
